name: A Governance Structure for AI
title: A Governance Structure for AI
answer: A governance structure for AI means a standing committee, not a one-time policy, that reviews tools, updates rules, and oversees pilots. It matters because published rules need someone to maintain them, and decisions made in private or rarely cannot guide adoption. The committee should include both skeptics and enthusiasts, and it should be ready to remove a tool that fails.

sections.body: Rules about AI in a district do not maintain themselves, so many districts create an AI committee to do that work. Its members typically include teachers, principals, technology and privacy staff, special education and English learner specialists, and parents, and students can serve too, especially in high school. The committee reviews tools, updates the rules, and oversees pilots. The problem it solves is drift and secrecy: a committee that meets rarely or keeps its decisions private cannot guide adoption. Clear authority and a regular schedule are what turn a written policy into a working one.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or district, the committee runs on a set rhythm. It might meet monthly to review requests for new tools and quarterly to review how pilots are going. Its decisions are published so everyone can see which tools are approved and why. Membership is deliberately balanced, with skeptics alongside enthusiasts, because skeptics raise hard questions about privacy, equity, and evidence that enthusiasts may skip. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond noting that students can serve, especially at the high school level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea. It rests on practice and on the judgment of the districts that form these committees, not on research cited in the chapter. The claims made are practical ones: a committee of only enthusiasts risks approving tools too quickly, and balanced membership produces better decisions and more trust. These are stated as reasoning about how governance works, not as measured results.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Governance also means knowing when to stop. A tool that fails a pilot, loses its privacy agreement, or harms students should be removed promptly, and the committee should apply the exit criteria described in Chapter 4 without hesitation. The limits are built into the structure: the committee needs clear authority and a regular schedule, and its decisions must be published, or it cannot guide adoption. The decisions themselves stay with people on the committee, who weigh privacy, equity, and evidence. Nothing here is legal advice; it describes practice.
